title: Can criterion-referencing work?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou examines the popular claim that criterion-referencing is the fairest way to grade national exams, because it ties results to curriculum standards instead of to the performance of other students. She argues it has serious practical and theoretical problems. Even tightly defined criteria, such as comparing two fractions, can be targeted by questions of wildly different difficulty, and examiners cannot predict in advance how hard a question will be or where a pass mark should fall. The problem grows with extended writing criteria, and New Zealand's strongly criterion-referenced system produced a dramatic fall in pass rates. She closes on the philosophical point, citing William Angoff, that norms may lurk behind most criteria, as with historical units of measurement.
points: Criterion-referencing sounds fair because it rewards individual attainment regardless of peers, but it depends on criteria that can be interpreted in very different ways.
Questions aimed at the same criterion can differ greatly in difficulty, and examiners struggle to predict difficulty or set pass marks in advance.
Vague criteria for extended writing make the problem worse.
New Zealand's adoption of a strong criterion-referenced system caused a sharp drop in pass rates from one year to the next.
Angoff's argument that norms lurk behind criteria is illustrated by measurement history, where each new standard rests on a new kind of norm.
quotes: Criterion-referencing is often maintained to be the best method as it allows for exam performance to be explicitly linked to curriculum content and standards. It rewards the performance of the individual regardless of the performance of their peers.

Many alternative methods of assessment rely on some kind of norm: the performance of the current or a previous group of students. This seems less fair as it means an individual’s performance is defined in terms of what others can do, not in terms of what they can do.

Examiners basically find it impossible to predict in advance how difficult a particular question will be, and similarly find it impossible to predict in advance what mark on a test should constitute a pass grade.

And remember, 'can compare two fractions to see which is larger' is a relatively precisely defined criterion. How much more of a problem will this be when you are trying to mark extended writing using criteria like 'can use vocabulary with originality and flair'?
When New Zealand adopted a strong criterion-referenced system about 20 years ago, it led to a dramatic fall in pass rates from one year to the next.

The history of modern measurement is the attempt to ground measurements in something more absolute and less arbitrary. The problem is that every new method you come up with arguably just depends on a new kind of norm.
